rationale: A live probe confirms https://consensus.app/llms.txt returns HTTP 200 with a structured product summary. Missing for 10: per-page markdown doc variants (the .md probe returned 404) and independent corroboration of agents using these files.

Consensus documents an AI-powered Library workspace where users import their own papers (Zotero, BibTeX, PDF, RIS) and then search, find gaps, and put the collection to work. Around that sit in-product AI synthesis with citations, Consensus Meter aggregation, PICO extraction and Citation Graph suggestions of related work. This covers AI-generated insights and suggestions inside the product, but the specifics of what it surfaces from a user's own library are thin marketing claims. Missing for 10: detailed documentation of the insight and suggestion outputs generated over the user's own library, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Nothing in the evidence shows Consensus offering user-configurable automations that run on their own in the background, such as scheduled searches, alerts, or recurring jobs. The REST API and MCP server, including the claim of running "automated searches with our API", are developer building blocks a user would have to wire into their own automation. The research agent chains tools within an interactive session, which is not background automation.

Consensus documents a built-in research agent that chains citation crawling, DOI lookup, author search and similar-paper discovery. Deep Search produces literature reviews in minutes, and Threads supports conversational follow-up, so users can hand research tasks to the in-product AI. Missing for 10: detailed documentation of how tasks are scoped, executed and reviewed by the agent, and any independent or hands-on corroboration of how well delegation works.

Consensus documents a REST API and an MCP server that expose the same retrieval and synthesis surface as the web app, and it markets the API for running automated searches inside custom workflows and agent pipelines. That amounts to first-party headless, programmatic operation, and its documented parameters (e.g. excludePreprints) confirm the surface is scriptable. Missing for 10: a CLI or CI-specific integration guidance (auth tokens, rate limits, pipeline examples), and independent or hands-on corroboration of headless automation.

Consensus positions itself as an AI research agent, so letting users connect external MCP servers is a fair question for this kind of product. That is the server role and earns no credit here; nothing documents users plugging third-party MCP servers into Consensus to use their tools.

Hands-on reports corroborate this multi-step behavior: 3-6 minute searches, good follow-up questions, a 'Discovery Progress and Exhaustiveness' readout, and comprehensive topic coverage. Missing for 10: documentation exposing the intermediate investigation steps to the user, and consistent depth on niche or gray-literature queries (one user saw a refined search return nearly the same results; another saw much gray literature missed).

The evidence never documents exporting results to documents, spreadsheets, or reference-manager formats such as BibTeX, RIS, or CSV. What it does show are adjacent features that are not exports: Markdown notes and reports created inside the workspace, custom tables, folders, and stars. The API and MCP access are developer building blocks rather than an export capability.

There is no explicit free-tier doc, but the pricing copy promises "10x higher usage limits" on a higher plan, implying a lower-limit base tier. Community users describe trying searches after a "Try it now" sign-up, and one mentions a $20/month paid tier. Sign-up is gated on an institutional or company email, and an independent researcher reported being unable to sign up, so not every researcher can try it. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of a free tier or trial and its quotas, clarity on how many free searches a researcher gets, and open sign-up without an institutional email.

First-party docs say users can 'trace any statement by following in-line citations back to the source paper.' Generated notes and reports carry citations that link back to source papers, and deep reviews produce a written synthesis tied to a ranked paper list. A community user also praised Undermind for reliably returning references, unlike general LLMs. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on confirmation that in-line citations accurately support each claim, and in-depth documentation of how citation granularity works (e.g., passage-level anchoring).

Undermind documents a deep literature review that plans its own searches, follows citations and authors, and stops only when new searches stop finding relevant papers. Its notifications, however, are alerts about newly published papers on monitored topics, an adjacent feature that does not notify you when a research job finishes. Missing for 10: documented notification when a job's result is ready, evidence that jobs keep running after the user leaves the session, any job-status or background-queue mechanism.

Undermind's homepage directly claims you can 'get notified whenever relevant papers are published,' and the enterprise page describes 'role-aware alerts' that monitor saved topics and send updates. Both match standing searches that surface new sources. The evidence, however, is marketing-level only. missing for 10: detailed docs on how alerts are set up and configured (frequency, delivery channel, query scope), clarity on whether alerts exist outside the enterprise tier, independent or hands-on corroboration that alerts work.

Undermind's own MCP server exposes much of the core UI functionality programmatically: deep literature reviews, search with filters, bulk DOI and title resolution, author lookup, full-text PDF Q&A, workspace notes, folders and starring. A separate enterprise-only programmatic API with batch processing is claimed but not documented, and probes found no OpenAPI spec. Nothing shows that UI-only features (topic alerts, follow-up clarifying questions, custom tables, shared-workspace collaboration, team management, sort/filter of results) are reachable programmatically, so full UI parity is not established. missing for 10: documented public REST API/OpenAPI spec, programmatic access to alerts, team/workspace administration and collaboration, custom table generation, an explicit parity statement, independent hands-on corroboration of API/MCP coverage.

Requesting removal of organization data is deletion, not export. Markdown notes stored in the workspace, plus MCP and API access, are adjacent features or developer building blocks rather than a documented bulk export in open formats.

Missing for 10: explicit support for uploading an arbitrary personal corpus (non-paper documents, bulk ingestion), evidence that the deep-research agent can be scoped to only the user's uploaded corpus, detailed upload docs, and independent or hands-on corroboration.
